title: The New Congress Must Rein in Trump’s Dangerous China Policy
summary: Trump’s accommodating approach toward China has emboldened Beijing, but the new Congress has a rare chance to change course.

Since returning to the White House, President Trump has gambled that if Washington took a[more accommodating stance](https://www.reaganfoundation.org/reagan-institute/publications/slouching-toward-beijing-the-trump-xi-summit-and-the-trajectory-of-us-china-strat) toward China’s ambitions in Asia, Beijing would respond with restraint.


The Trump administration has scaled back key military operations in the region and withheld support for Taiwan and U.S. allies facing Chinese coercion. The hope has been that such measures would help avert a potential clash with China. But nearly two years into his second term, Mr. Trump’s approach is backfiring, emboldening China to throw its weight around Asia and raising the risk of a military crisis.


The Democratic victory in the U.S. midterm elections offers a critical opportunity for change. With control of both chambers of Congress, Democrats will have the power to put guardrails around the president’s failing China policy — and they may not have to do it alone.


For years, Republicans in Congress were among the strongest voices for[standing up to Beijing,](https://www.washingtonpost.com/national-security/2025/10/24/xi-jinping-trump-china-summit/) yet many have stayed quiet to avoid challenging the president. The unmistakable rebuke that voters delivered to Mr. Trump this month may change that calculus by giving Republicans more leeway to work with Democrats toward a course correction on China.


The new Congress must move quickly to assert its constitutional power over spending, oversight and confirmation of presidential appointments to limit the damage the administration can do in its final two years and build an approach to Asia that allies can count on and that Beijing has to take seriously.


Breaking with past administrations, the president has played down the notion of strategic competition with China in favor of what both Beijing and Washington now[describe](https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2026/09/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-advances-a-fair-and-reciprocal-relationship-with-china-while-hosting-historic-state-visit/) as a “constructive relationship of strategic stability.” That shift will frame the conversation during[a series of summits](https://www.afp.com/en/global-powers-head-asia-trade-ai-security-focus) in Asia that Mr. Trump will attend this week, including a meeting of Southeast Asian leaders in Manila, followed by a wider Asia-Pacific gathering in China where he is expected to meet President Xi Jinping for the third time this year.
